details:
**"The Wife of Bath's Tale" and "what women most desire"**
A knight of King Arthur's court rapes a maiden and is sentenced to death. The queen spares him on condition that he discover what women most desire within a year and a day. An ugly old hag gives him the answer, sovereignty (mastery over their husbands), in exchange for his promise to marry her. When he lets her choose whether to be ugly and faithful or beautiful and possibly unfaithful, she becomes both beautiful and true. The tale opens by recalling that in Arthur's day Britain was full of fairies and elves.

**Palamon, Arcite, and Emelye in "The Knight's Tale"**
The first tale, told by the Knight. Theseus marches on Thebes after Creon refuses to let the widows bury their dead, and he imprisons the Theban cousins Palamon and Arcite in a tower. From the tower, both fall in love with Emelye as they watch her gathering flowers in a garden. After release, Arcite returns in disguise as a page named Philostrate. Arcite wins the tournament for her hand but is thrown from his horse and dies, so Palamon marries Emelye. Theseus delivers the philosophical "First Mover" speech near the end.

**The Tabard Inn, Harry Bailly, and the storytelling contest**
The frame story: about thirty pilgrims gather at the Tabard Inn in Southwark. The Host, Harry Bailly, proposes that each tell tales on the road, promising a free supper at the end to whoever tells the best story, and he judges and often interrupts them. Chaucer completed only 24 tales, and the framed structure is often compared to Boccaccio's Decameron.

**The Wife of Bath's Prologue**
Alisoun, the gap-toothed Wife of Bath, boasts of her five husbands and argues for women's authority in marriage. Her fifth husband, the young clerk Jankyn, read to her from a book of wicked wives; she tore pages out of it, and he struck her so hard that she went deaf in one ear. In her tale, she retells Ovid's story of King Midas's ears, making Midas's wife the one who cannot keep the secret and whispers it into a marsh.

**The shrine of Thomas Becket**
The pilgrims are traveling to Canterbury Cathedral to visit the shrine of the "holy blissful martyr" Saint Thomas Becket, the archbishop murdered in 1170, who "helped them when they were sick."

**"When April with his showers sweet..."**
The famous opening of the General Prologue, in Middle English "Whan that Aprill with his shoures soote / The droghte of March hath perced to the roote." It describes April's showers bathing every vein in liquor, the "sweet breath" of Zephyrus, and "small fowls" making melody that sleep all night with open eye, before people long to go on pilgrimages.

**"The Miller's Tale": Nicholas, Alisoun, and the tubs**
A bawdy tale in which the student Nicholas convinces the old carpenter John that a second Noah's flood is coming. John hangs three tubs from the ceiling to float away in, and while he sleeps in his, Nicholas sleeps with John's young wife Alisoun. When John hears the cry for "water," he cuts the rope, crashes to the floor, and breaks his arm.

**Absolon and the hot coulter**
In "The Miller's Tale," the foppish parish clerk Absolon, who also loves Alisoun, is tricked at the window into kissing her backside. He returns with a red-hot coulter (plow blade) from the blacksmith. When Nicholas sticks his rear out the window and farts in his face, Absolon brands him on the buttocks.

**"The Pardoner's Tale" and the three rioters**
Three young revelers in Flanders set out to kill Death. An old man directs them to an oak tree, where they find nearly eight bushels of gold florins. Two stab the third, who had poisoned their wine, so all three die. Afterward the Pardoner tries to sell his fake relics, and the Host retorts that he would like to have the Pardoner's testicles enshrined in a hog's turd.

**"The Nun's Priest's Tale" and Chauntecleer**
A beast fable in which the proud rooster Chauntecleer dreams of danger, which his wife, the hen Pertelote, dismisses. The fox flatters him into closing his eyes and crowing, then seizes him. Chauntecleer tricks the fox into turning to taunt his pursuers, then escapes into a tree. It follows "The Monk's Tale," a string of tragedies that the Knight interrupts.

**"The Franklin's Tale": Dorigen and the rocks of Brittany**
Dorigen, wife of the knight Arveragus, rashly promises the squire Aurelius her love if he removes all the rocks from the coast of Brittany. Aurelius pays a magician-clerk to make them seem to vanish, and her husband tells her she must keep her word. Seeing such generosity, Aurelius releases her from the promise, and the clerk forgives Aurelius's debt.

**"Sir Thopas" and "not worth a turd"**
The pilgrim Chaucer's own deliberately terrible rhyming tale about the knight Sir Thopas, who seeks an elf-queen and meets the three-headed giant Sir Olifaunt. The Host cuts it off, crying "no more of this," and says his rhyming is "not worth a turd." Chaucer then tells the prose "Tale of Melibee."

**The Miller, the Reeve, and "quiting"**
The pilgrims often "quite" (pay back) each other with insulting stories. The Reeve, a carpenter, answers the Miller's tale of a fooled carpenter with a tale about the cheating miller Symkyn. In it, two Cambridge students get revenge by sleeping with his wife and daughter, moving a baby's cradle so the wife climbs into the wrong bed.

**The Friar's and Summoner's Tales**
The Friar and the Summoner trade insulting tales. In the Friar's, a greedy summoner tries to extort an old widow, who damns him to the Devil, and the devil drags him, body and soul, off to hell (she also damns her frying pan). In the Summoner's, a sick man named Thomas tells a greedy friar he has a gift hidden beneath him and farts into the friar's hand.

**"The Merchant's Tale," "The Manciple's Tale," and "The Prioress's Tale"**
In "The Merchant's Tale," the old knight January marries young May, who cheats on him with the squire Damian in a pear tree. In "The Manciple's Tale," the god Phoebus kills his unfaithful wife after his white crow reveals her adultery, then plucks out the crow's feathers and turns it black. In "The Prioress's Tale," a murdered Christian boy keeps singing "Alma redemptoris mater" until a grain is removed from his tongue.
